noodles/8130199:
D28's room shipped as an oscillator. A friend's iPhone found it: press
play, and about ten seconds later the whole mix runs away. It was never
an iPhone bug - it reproduces in desktop Chrome on the first probe, and
it has been in every roll since D28, hiding in the audit's own dice
table as loudness spread (3.47 dB, one roll pinned at PSR -0.31).

Two causes, one mistake twice: asking Web Audio for something it does
not mean by it.

The damper. For a lowpass or highpass the API prices Q in DECIBELS of
resonance rather than as a linear Q - the spec's own
alpha = sin(w0)/(2*10^(Q/20)) - so Q 0.5 asked for half a dB of boost
and got a peak of +1.59 dB at 1.9 kHz. Inside a comb at fb 0.86 that is
a loop gain of 1.033: the room climbed 6.4 dB/s and pinned the master
flat against the ceiling. Butterworth is -3.01 in those units,
maximally flat at every frequency, so the loop gain is the 0.86 the
RT60 arithmetic already assumed. Tone.Filter clamps Q positive and
throws on a Butterworth one, so the node is a Tone.BiquadFilter.

The allpasses. A Schroeder allpass taps one delay from inside its
feedback loop and from outside it, and Web Audio does not promise those
two taps are the same sample: a browser may add latency to break a
cycle, and Chrome decides that per graph rather than per structure.
Five identical renders of the room came back -6.60, -4.58, -4.58,
-4.53, -4.58 dB of impulse energy. An allpass preserves energy, so only
-6.60 was one. The four combs alone render bit-identically, so the
allpasses are out and the room is four damped combs, RT60 2.02 s: less
lush, and the same on every device. Diffusion comes back the day the
room moves into one worklet, which is where Tone kept Freeverb's combs
and allpasses for exactly this reason.

The return is re-matched by measurement, 0.006 to 0.52: +1.12 dB
against a dry strip at a wide-open send, where the old Freeverb read
+1.08, so the send fader keeps the wet/dry ratio it had. The old number
could not have been right at
